approaches.name: Lateral approach to the humeral shaft
aliases: lateral paratricipital approach to the humerus
approaches.corridor: Lateral interval along the lateral intermuscular septum, identifying the radial nerve and following it to expose the distal two-thirds of the humerus

sources.title: Lateral approach to the humeral shaft
Posterior triceps-split approach to the humeral shaft

procedure_applications.condition: A distal-two-thirds humeral shaft fracture is plated through a lateral exposure with radial nerve control

positioning.text: Position supine or lateral with the arm supported and the whole humerus from deltoid insertion to lateral epicondyle accessible.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the deltoid insertion, the lateral epicondyle, and the lateral intermuscular septum.

incision.text: Follow a line from the deltoid insertion to the lateral epicondyle, extending proximally along the anterior or posterior deltoid margin as needed.

superficial_interval.text: Incise the deep fascia posterior to the lateral intermuscular septum and enter the posterior compartment between triceps and the septum, developing the plane from distal to proximal.

deep_interval.text: Identify the posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve and follow it proximally to the radial nerve, find the radial nerve in the fat adjacent to triceps in the middle third, and distally follow it between brachialis and brachioradialis.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, deep fascia, the lateral intermuscular septum, the radial nerve, and the humeral shaft.

structures_at_risk.text: The radial nerve, crossing from posterior to anterior across the mid-humerus, is the principal structure at risk and must be identified and protected.

danger_zones.text: The mid-humeral segment where the radial nerve crosses is the danger zone; identify the nerve before working on bone there.

retraction_hazards.text: Retract the radial nerve gently and avoid stretching it while exposing the underlying bone.

exposure.text: Exposes the distal two-thirds of the humerus and can extend proximally to the proximal humerus.

limitations.text: Proximal extension along the deltopectoral interval does not reach the proximal radial nerve, and posterior deltoid extension gives more limited bone exposure.

indications.text: Indicated for plating of distal-two-thirds humeral shaft fractures where radial nerve control is required.

closure.text: Ensure the radial nerve lies in a healthy soft-tissue bed and close the incision in layers in the standard manner.

complications.text: The main complication is radial nerve palsy; wound problems may also occur.

questions.question: How is the radial nerve first located in the lateral humeral approach?
questions.answer: By finding the posterior antebrachial cutaneous nerve and following it proximally to the radial nerve.

questions.question: Between which muscles is the radial nerve followed distally?
How much of the humerus does the lateral approach expose?
questions.answer: The distal two-thirds, with possible proximal extension.

approaches.name: Posterior triceps-split approach to the humeral shaft
aliases: posterior approach to the humerus (triceps split)
approaches.corridor: Posterior midline split between and through the triceps heads, identifying the radial nerve and profunda brachii in the spiral groove, to expose the posterior humerus

sources.title: Posterior triceps-split approach to the humeral shaft
Lateral approach to the humeral shaft

procedure_applications.condition: A distal-half humeral shaft fracture is plated posteriorly
A B1 or C periprosthetic humeral fracture with a stable retained stem in the distal half is plated posteriorly after the radial nerve is identified

positioning.text: Position prone or lateral with the arm over a bolster and the elbow flexed so the posterior arm is presented.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the tip of the olecranon and the posterior midline of the arm.

incision.text: Make a midline posterior incision starting at the olecranon and running proximally in a straight line along the posterior arm.

superficial_interval.text: Proximally develop the interval between the lateral and long heads of the triceps; distally split the common triceps tendon sharply along the line of the incision.

deep_interval.text: Identify the radial nerve and accompanying profunda brachii artery in the spiral groove, since the exposure crosses the radial nerve in the mid-humeral region, and protect the ulnar nerve medially.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, triceps tendon and muscle, the radial nerve and profunda brachii in the spiral groove, and the posterior humerus.

structures_at_risk.text: The radial nerve and profunda brachii in the spiral groove and the ulnar nerve medially, constrained where it passes through the medial intermuscular septum, are at risk.

danger_zones.text: The spiral groove where the incision crosses the radial nerve is the danger zone; identify the nerve before proximal dissection.

retraction_hazards.text: Protect the radial nerve during triceps mobilization and keep the ulnar nerve free medially.

exposure.text: Exposes the posterior humerus from the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery proximally to the capitellum distally.

limitations.text: Distal exposure is limited by the triceps tendon split, so a distal posterior triceps-sparing approach may be preferred very distally.

indications.text: Indicated for fractures involving the distal half of the humerus fixed posteriorly, including B1 and C periprosthetic fractures with a stable retained stem; more proximal periprosthetic work requires identifying the radial nerve first.

closure.text: Repair the split triceps tendon and close the incision in layers in the standard manner.

complications.text: Complications include radial nerve palsy, ulnar nerve irritation, and triceps weakness.

questions.question: Which structures accompany the radial nerve in the spiral groove?
How is the triceps managed proximally versus distally?
questions.answer: Proximally the interval between the lateral and long heads is developed; distally the common tendon is split.

questions.question: Which nerve must be protected medially in the posterior approach?

approaches.name: Extended deltopectoral approach to the humeral shaft
aliases: extended anterior deltopectoral approach to the humerus
approaches.corridor: Deltopectoral interval extended distally along the lateral biceps to expose the anterior humeral shaft between the musculocutaneous and radial nerve territories

sources.title: Extended deltopectoral approach to the humeral shaft
Lateral approach to the humeral shaft
Anterior Brachialis Splitting Approach To Humerus

procedure_applications.condition: A proximal four-fifths humeral shaft fracture is exposed anteriorly

positioning.text: Position supine (beach-chair) with the arm draped free and the shoulder to distal humerus accessible.

surface_landmarks.text: Mark the coracoid process, the proximal humeral shaft at the axilla, the midshaft, and the radial epicondyle.

incision.text: Start at the coracoid process and follow the humeral shaft distally toward the lateral epicondyle.

superficial_interval.text: Open the deltopectoral groove, retract the cephalic vein laterally, and develop the plane between deltoid and pectoralis major, incising the clavipectoral fascia lateral to the conjoined tendon.

deep_interval.text: Extend distally between the biceps/brachialis and the mobile wad, identify the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm, and where needed mobilize the radial nerve as it perforates the lateral intermuscular septum distally.

layers.text: Skin, subcutaneous tissue, the deltopectoral interval with the cephalic vein, clavipectoral fascia, the anterior humerus, and distally the brachialis split.

structures_at_risk.text: The axillary nerve under proximal retractors, the musculocutaneous nerve entering coracobrachialis as close as 2.5 cm from the coracoid, the radial nerve in the distal two-fifths, and the cephalic vein are at risk.

danger_zones.text: Retractors under the conjoined tendon endanger the musculocutaneous nerve, and Hohmann retractors in the distal two-fifths of the humerus carry a high risk of radial nerve injury.

retraction_hazards.text: Position Roux or Hohmann retractors carefully to avoid the axillary nerve proximally and the radial nerve distally, and avoid vigorous retraction under the conjoined tendon.

exposure.text: Exposes almost any humeral shaft fracture involving the proximal four-fifths of the humerus.

limitations.text: The approach does not give good access to the most distal humerus or the distal radial nerve, which may require a separate lateral exposure.

indications.text: Indicated for plating of proximal and midshaft humeral fractures involving the proximal four-fifths.

closure.text: Irrigate, optionally place a drain under the deltoid, preserve the cephalic vein, and close in layers.

complications.text: Complications relate mainly to nerve injury: axillary nerve from proximal retractors, musculocutaneous neurapraxia from conjoined-tendon retraction, and radial nerve injury from distal retractors.

questions.question: How close to the coracoid can the musculocutaneous nerve enter coracobrachialis?
questions.answer: As close as 2.5 cm distal to the tip of the coracoid.

questions.question: Which retractor placement carries a high risk of radial nerve injury?
questions.answer: Hohmann retractors in the distal two-fifths of the humerus.

questions.question: Which vein marks the deltopectoral interval and should be preserved?
